content:
Two verses draw the same challenge. The Quran says some Jews called Ezra the son of God. It says Jesus will be asked whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods. Critics ask for the Jews and the Christians who believed either, and they say that the Quran has misunderstood both religions.

The objection matters because it goes to the source of the Quran. If the book misdescribes the beliefs of its neighbours, the critic argues, it cannot have come from a God who knows them. A Muslim reply has to show what each verse actually claims, and then whether that claim fits what is known of Jews and Christians in and around Arabia in the seventh century.

One of these has a clear answer. The other is a real difficulty, and I will treat it as one. The entries below take the Mary verse first, then the Ezra verse, and in each case they state the objection at its strongest before replying.

The verse has God asking Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as two gods besides God, and Jesus denying it.[1] There is no mention of a Trinity in that verse, and no claim that Christians define God as Father, Son and Mary.

The Quran does address the Trinity, separately, when it rejects saying God is the third of three.[2] It also describes Mary in the next verses as a truthful woman who, like her son, ate food, which is a statement about her humanity.[2] Merging the verses into "Muslims think Mary is in the Trinity" creates a claim the text does not make. The critic's best point is that no Christian church teaches that Mary is God. That is correct, and the verse does not say otherwise. It is a question put to Jesus on the Day of Judgement about whether he ever authorised worship of himself and his mother.

Jesus's answer in the verse sets its tone: "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right." He goes on to say that he told them only what God commanded him, to worship God, his Lord and theirs.[1] The scene is a trial of what was done in his name, held on the Day of Judgement, and its subject is worship.

The Quran uses the language of "taking as gods" for practice as well as doctrine. Another verse says that Jews and Christians took their scholars and monks as lords besides God.[3] When Adi ibn Hatim, a former Christian, objected to the Prophet that they had not worshipped their monks, the Prophet asked whether they had not accepted as lawful what the monks made lawful and as forbidden what they forbade. Adi said that they had, and the Prophet said, "That is worshipping them."[4] On this usage, a verse about taking Mary as a god does not require a creed that calls her God. It requires a practice that gives her what belongs to God.

Epiphanius of Salamis, writing around 376, describes women in Arabia who offered cakes to Mary as a goddess, and he rebukes them for worshipping her.[5] Some scholars doubt the sect existed as he describes it.

The point does not depend on that sect. The verse asks whether Mary was taken as a god. That is a question about worship, and the history of Marian devotion is long enough that a church father felt the need to warn against it.

Epiphanius called the group the Collyridians, after the small loaves (kollyris) they offered. Whatever their numbers, his warning shows that a church father on the edge of the Arab world thought the danger of treating Mary as divine real enough to argue against at length. By the sixth century, hymns and icons in honour of Mary filled the churches of the Byzantine and Syriac worlds, and petitions addressed directly to her were part of popular piety. The Quran addressed a world in which that piety was familiar to its hearers.

Christians reply, with reason, that their churches distinguish the worship owed to God from the honour given to Mary, and that the Council of Ephesus in 431, which called her Theotokos ("bearer of God"), spoke about the person of Christ and not about Mary's divinity.[6] The verse is consistent with that reply. It speaks of what ordinary believers may do, and its target is any practice that treats her as a rival to God, whatever the doctrine says.

The Quran reports that some Jews said Ezra is the son of God.[7] No surviving Jewish text says this in those words. That is the honest starting point, and a Muslim who pretends otherwise hands the critic an easy win.

The strongest form of the objection adds that the Quran goes on to say that in this the Jews and the Christians "imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them".[7] If the verse were a mistake, the critic argues, the Prophet's Jewish opponents in Medina would have denied it loudly, and the sources would record their denial. The sources record no such denial. That silence is weak evidence either way, but it is consistent with the commentators' view that the saying was known among some of the Jews the Prophet met.

Jewish readers rightly add that mainstream Judaism has never taught that Ezra is divine, and that the charge has been painful to hear. The Quran's wording is general: "the Jews say". A Muslim answer cannot rest on proving that Judaism held this belief. It has to rest on two narrower claims, that the verse points at a particular group and that such a belief is imaginable in the language of the age.

Classical exegetes read the verse as describing a particular group within Judaism. The tradition names Sallam ibn Mishkam and his companions, Jews of Medina who disputed with the Prophet, among those who said it.[8] The Quran often names a whole community for the speech of some of its members, and the commentators read this verse in the same way.

The absence of a surviving Jewish text also proves less than it seems. As the historian F. E. Peters observed, the Quran is very nearly the only source for what Jews in seventh-century Arabia believed.[9] A belief held by one community in Medina could leave no trace in the rabbinic literature of Babylon and Palestine. The reverse also holds: the Medinan sources that report the saying are late, and they do not independently confirm it. A fair reader keeps both facts in view.

Some later Muslim writers tried to locate the group. Ibn Hazm, who knew a great deal about the Jewish communities of his time, attributed the saying to a sect in Yemen.[10] His report, like the Medinan tradition, cannot be checked against Jewish sources, and it shows that Muslim scholars themselves treated the verse as describing a particular group and not Judaism as a whole.

Ezra is remembered as the man who restored the Torah after the exile. The Talmud says that he was worthy of having the Torah given through him, had Moses not come first.[11] A text circulating in the early centuries has God tell him that he will be taken up from among men, to live with God's son.[12] Scholars debate how that word should be translated, and the Latin text is later than the languages it came from.

"Son of God" was also a title that Jewish scripture applied to Israel and its kings, and Jewish writings called angels the children of God.[13] The Quran knows the idiom as a claim to nearness, since it quotes both Jews and Christians as saying "we are the children of God and His beloved".[14] An exaltation of Ezra expressed in that vocabulary, among one community, is not far-fetched.

Jewish literature also shows how far the exaltation of a human figure could go. The Book of Enoch known as 3 Enoch describes Enoch being transformed into the angel Metatron and given the title "the lesser YHWH".[15] The Talmud tells of the rabbi Elisha ben Abuya, who saw Metatron seated in heaven and concluded that there might be "two powers" there, a conclusion the rabbis condemned.[16] These texts are mystical and their dates are debated, and they concern Enoch. They show that a scribe-hero of Israel could be raised in some circles to a status that mainstream Judaism rejected. Gordon Newby, a historian of the Jews of Arabia, has suggested that Arabian Jewish groups may have held such traditions about Ezra.[17]

It is also not proven. Honesty requires saying both.

There is also a lesson in method here. A Muslim who answers every objection with equal confidence loses credibility on the ones that are well answered. The Mary verse rests on the text itself and on a well-documented history of devotion. The Ezra verse rests on a narrower base: the Medinan tradition, the commentators and the vocabulary of exaltation in Jewish writing. Saying so is part of answering it honestly.

The bottom line

On Mary, the objection attacks a claim the Quran does not make. The verse concerns what Jesus authorised, it says nothing about Trinitarian doctrine, and the history of devotion to Mary gives it a plain context. On Ezra, the absence of a surviving text is real, and the answer rests on the verse's first audience and on Ezra's standing in Jewish memory.

One verse is answered. The other is argued, and a Muslim may legitimately say that the evidence outside the Quran is thin. Know which is which before you debate either.
